label: A16
title: Chapter 16: Measurement Theory – Constructs, Validity, and Reliability

blocks.html:
1. A new depression screening questionnaire for elderly rural patients is adapted word-for-word from a validated questionnaire for urban working-age adults, without any local review. Which type of validity is most directly at risk, and why?

Content validity: whether the items cover the construct fully and appropriately for this population. The way depression shows itself, the idioms used to describe it and the relevant life domains differ by age and culture. Items about work stress may not apply to elderly rural patients, and locally common expressions of distress (for example, bodily complaints) may be missing. An expert and community review, with cultural adaptation (§16.7), is needed before use.

2. A clinician glances at a new anxiety scale and says “these questions look like they measure anxiety.” Which more limited type of validity does this comment support?

Face validity only: a surface impression that the instrument appears to measure what it claims. It is weaker than content validity, which needs a systematic expert review of whether the items cover the whole construct.

1. A new physical activity scale correlates at r = 0.85 with an existing validated physical activity scale, and at r = −0.30 with a sedentary-behaviour screen (a related but distinct construct). Which strand of validity does each finding support? Why is the second comparison more informative than a correlation with shoe size would be?

The r = 0.85 with another physical-activity measure supports convergent validity. The much weaker r = −0.30 with a sedentary-behaviour screen supports discriminant validity: the new scale is not simply the reverse of “sitting”. Both are strands of construct validity. Sedentary behaviour is a construct a critic could plausibly confuse with physical activity, so a clear gap between 0.85 and a correlation of only −0.30 is informative. Nobody expects physical activity to track shoe size, so a near-zero correlation with it would confirm nothing.

2. A new scale to predict medication adherence correlates well with adherence measured six months later. Which form of validity is this, and how does it differ from correlating with adherence measured on the same day?

Predictive validity: the criterion is measured in the future. Correlation with adherence measured at the same time would be concurrent validity. Both are forms of criterion validity, told apart by when the criterion is measured.

3. A tool predicting low birthweight is given at 20 weeks to 250 women. Of 40 babies later born under 2.5 kg, 30 mothers had screened positive; of 210 others, 42 had screened positive. Compute the sensitivity and specificity. Why are these reported instead of r?

  1. Sensitivity = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75.
  2. Specificity = (210 − 42) ÷ 210 = 168 ÷ 210 = 0.80.

The criterion (low birthweight, yes/no) is binary, and the tool is used to classify. Predictive validity is therefore reported as sensitivity and specificity (and predictive values, or AUC for a continuous score), not a correlation (§16.2.3.2).

1. A researcher gives the same questionnaire to the same patients twice, two weeks apart, and finds a high correlation. Which type of reliability is this? Name one threat that would inflate the estimate and one that would deflate it, even for a well-designed instrument.

Test-retest reliability. Inflating: respondents remember and repeat their first answers (memory or practice effects), especially with a short interval. Deflating: real change in the construct between occasions (for example, a patient’s anxiety actually improving), or an intervening event such as health education. A low value does not by itself show the instrument is unreliable. Note also that a correlation ignores a systematic shift between occasions, so ICC(2,1) is preferred (§16.3.2).

2. A four-item scale has item variances 1.2, 1.0, 1.5 and 1.3 and total-score variance 12.0. Compute Cronbach’s alpha. A ten-item scale has α = 0.97. What might this very high value signal?

  1. Σsᵢ² = 1.2 + 1.0 + 1.5 + 1.3 = 5.0.
  2. α = [4 ÷ 3] × (1 − 5.0 ÷ 12.0) = 1.333 × 0.583 = 0.78, satisfactory for group comparisons by the Bland & Altman (1997) convention.

α = 0.97 on ten items may mean redundancy: several items ask the same question in different words, adding length without new information. Terwee et al. (2007) rate α positively only up to 0.95. Also, α rises with the number of items (Spearman–Brown), so a high value partly reflects length. It does not show that the scale is unidimensional or valid.

3. Two nurses classify 200 children as “fever” or “no fever” by touch. Both say fever for 30, neither for 140, nurse A only for 20, nurse B only for 10. Compute pₒ, pₑ and κ, and give the Landis & Koch label.

  1. pₒ = (30 + 140) ÷ 200 = 0.85.
  2. Nurse A says fever for (30 + 20) ÷ 200 = 0.25; nurse B for (30 + 10) ÷ 200 = 0.20.
  3. pₑ = 0.25 × 0.20 + 0.75 × 0.80 = 0.05 + 0.60 = 0.65.
  4. κ = (0.85 − 0.65) ÷ (1 − 0.65) = 0.20 ÷ 0.35 = 0.57: “moderate” (0.41–0.60) on the Landis & Koch (1977) scale, a convention. Report the two marginal proportions too: nurse A calls fever more often (bias), and fever is the minority category (prevalence), both of which affect κ.

1. A new haemoglobinometer and the laboratory cyanmethaemoglobin method are compared in 40 pregnant women. Mean difference (new − lab) is −0.3 g/dL, SD of differences 0.6 g/dL. Compute the 95% limits of agreement. The study defines anaemia as Hb below 11 g/dL: interpret the limits for a woman whose laboratory value is 11.2 g/dL.

  1. Lower limit = −0.3 − 1.96 × 0.6 = −0.3 − 1.18 = −1.48 g/dL.
  2. Upper limit = −0.3 + 1.96 × 0.6 = −0.3 + 1.18 = 0.88 g/dL.

For about 95% of women, the new device reads between 1.48 g/dL below and 0.88 g/dL above the laboratory. For a woman whose laboratory value is 11.2 g/dL, the device could plausibly read anywhere from about 9.7 to 12.1 g/dL, so she could be labelled anaemic or not. The device under-reads on average (bias −0.3 g/dL) and is too imprecise to replace the laboratory for individual diagnosis near the cut-off, unless the investigators judged a difference of about 1.5 g/dL clinically acceptable beforehand.

2. The same study reports r = 0.96 between the two methods and concludes “excellent agreement”. What is wrong with this conclusion?

r measures how closely the points lie along some straight line, not whether the readings are equal. It would be 1 even if the device always read exactly 1 g/dL low. It also rises when the women’s true haemoglobin values vary widely, which says nothing about agreement. Agreement is assessed by the bias and limits of agreement (Bland & Altman, 1986), as in question 1.

1. A team runs PCA on 20 items meant to measure one construct, “quality of life”. Three components have eigenvalues above 1 (4.1, 1.3 and 1.1), explaining 20.5%, 6.5% and 5.5% of the variance. What do the percentages mean? What should the team check before concluding that the scale has three sub-dimensions?

With 20 standardised items the total variance is 20. Each percentage is the eigenvalue ÷ 20: the first component carries 4.1 ÷ 20 = 20.5% of the total variance, the next two 1.3 ÷ 20 = 6.5% and 1.1 ÷ 20 = 5.5%.

The eigenvalue > 1 (Kaiser) rule is a convention that can keep too many components. Before concluding there are three sub-dimensions, the team should:

  • inspect the scree plot and run parallel analysis. Here the first component dominates, and the next two only just exceed 1;
  • look at the loadings. Does each extra component have several items loading highly, with a sensible theme (for example, all the social-relationship items)? Or is it one or two items, or a method artefact such as all the negatively worded items loading together?
  • check the result against theory (for example, the WHOQOL domains) and, ideally, confirm the structure by CFA in a new sample.

If the three components prove real, report α and build scores for each sub-scale, not one total.

2. Explain why a highly reliable instrument is not automatically valid. A scale has reliability 0.64 and its criterion has reliability 0.81. What is the largest correlation the scale could show with the criterion?

Reliability is consistency. An instrument can consistently measure the wrong thing, like a scale that always reads 2 kg high. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

Largest possible correlation = √(r_xx × r_yy) = √(0.64 × 0.81) = √0.5184 = 0.72 (§16.4).

3. A Hindi translation of an English depression scale is to be used in Raipur. List the translation steps, and name two measurement properties you would test afresh, with the statistic for each.

Translation (Beaton et al., 2000): (1) two independent forward translations into Hindi; (2) synthesis of the two; (3) back-translation into English by a translator blind to the original; (4) expert committee review to agree a prefinal version; (5) pretest (cognitive interviews) in the target population.

Properties to test afresh, for example:

  • Internal consistency: Cronbach’s α per sub-scale, after checking structure by PCA/EFA (or CFA against the original structure).
  • Test-retest reliability: ICC(2,1), absolute agreement, over a suitable interval in at least 50 respondents (Terwee et al., 2007).
  • Criterion validity: sensitivity, specificity and AUC against a psychiatrist’s diagnostic interview.
  • Construct validity: predefined correlations, or known-groups comparisons (for example, attenders at a psychiatry OPD against community controls).
